name: Green Yellow
lede: Green Yellow is the electric yellow-green of the web keyword `greenyellow`, a name that sits on a border which older European color orders refused to draw: a yellow that leans toward green.

sections.title: A name made of two words
sections.body:
`greenyellow` is a keyword in CSS, the web's styling language, and it means #ADFF2F: red 173, green 255, blue 47 [8]. It comes from the X11 color set, the list of named colors that the X Window System handed on to early web browsers and that the W3C later wrote into its standards [8][9]. Paterson's dictionary of color lists it as one of the X11 colors, with the same hex code [5].

The name is a plain description, a green with yellow in it. Our color library files it that way, as a modifier name built from [[green]] and [[yellow]] rather than as a named thing [7].

sections.title: A hue that was hard to place
sections.body:
For most of European history a yellow that tended toward green did not fit any system [1][2]. Pastoureau notes that the order of colors attributed to Aristotle ran white, yellow, orange, red, green, blue, violet, black, and that in it yellow and green are not neighbors [1]. He asks how a yellow could lean toward green in such a sequence, and answers that it could lean toward orange, but not toward green [1].

Late medieval artists used a similar ladder, white, yellow, red, green, blue, purple, black, in which red separated green from yellow [2]. On that basis it made little sense to mix blue and yellow to get green, because the two were too far apart [2]. Only Newton's spectrum of 1666 put green between blue and yellow and let yellows stretch toward green [1][2].

Latin did have a word for a greenish yellow, *galbinus*. Pastoureau reports that it appeared late and probably derives from the Germanic word for yellow, *gelb* [1]. He leaves open whether it described a real intermediate shade or simply a yellow that Roman eyes found unpleasant [1]. Writers from Cicero to Juvenal ranged the yellows from orange to greenish, but still counted them as one color [1].

sections.title: Green and yellow together
sections.body:
Green and yellow side by side had a poor name in the late Middle Ages, though that is two colors in contrast, not a blend [3]. In images of the period, Judas is often dressed in green, yellow, or both [3]. In Shakespeare's day some actors balked at the green-and-yellow costume of clowns [3]. Pastoureau passes on a legend that many actors died after playing Judas, and suggests that toxic copper-acetate green dyes, not the role, may lie behind the tale [3].

The pairing eventually turned into a team color. Pastoureau notes that green and yellow came late to sports uniforms, and that in France two first-division football clubs only played in green and in yellow in the 1950s and 1960s [3].

sections.title: In the paint box
sections.body:
Reference books that classify historical materials by color keep a separate class for green-yellow. The Pigment Compendium uses it as one of its color classes, next to green and yellow [6]. Its entries include the dye plant buckthorn, whose unripe berries give a yellow dye and ripe berries a green one [6]. A nineteenth-century recipe it quotes warns that berries picked a little too green give an undesirable green yellow [6]. The same family of berries gave the medieval watercolor [[sap-green]] [10].

The Compendium also notes that goethite, the mineral behind yellow ochre, shifts from green-yellow to brown-yellow as its particles grow larger [6]. The color is therefore common in mineral and plant sources, even if the brilliant version on screens has no pigment equivalent.

sections.title: One of ten basic hues
sections.body:
Albert Munsell's system, which many painters use, divides the hue circle into ten steps, and green-yellow, written GY, is one of them, between yellow and green [4]. Gurney tells students of the system to learn all ten [4]. Our library computes the screen swatch as Munsell 6.8GY 9.2/16.2, a very light value with a very strong chroma [7].

That intensity is the point of this swatch. It is the top of the screen gamut for this hue, and no printing ink or painter's pigment of the kinds the books describe reaches it [7].

sections.title: The swatch and its neighbours
sections.body:
Other systems read the name more gently. Ridgway's 1912 plate V, hue 27, gives the pale, dull #E5E26D, and the 2010 xkcd survey produced two variants, #C9FF27 and #B5CE08 [7]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system calls the web swatch's neighborhood "brilliant yellow green", block 98, at a distance of 8.9 units [7].

The library lists five names within about two units of the web swatch: Lemon Green, Bright Yellow Green, French Lime, Green Lizard and Spring Bud [7]. The nearest name in our core list is [[lime]], about 3 units away [7]. [[chartreuse]] and [[acid-green]] are looser cousins.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
No painting in our archive of 23,781 museum paintings has this color covering as much as 1 per cent of its canvas, within four CIEDE2000 units of the swatch, as photographed [11]. That says something about the swatch, not about painting: it is a light-emitting screen color with almost no counterpart in aged, varnished paint [11].

As a phrase, *green yellow* is almost unchanged in Google Books from 1800 to the 1910s, rises from the 1920s, and peaks around 1940 [11]. The count includes plain lists such as "green, yellow, orange", so it overstates the color word [11].
